summary: For ages 9-11, a META / nature-of-science unit on monitoring volcanoes: learners name the warning signs volcanologists watch (rising gas emissions, ground swelling/bulging as magma moves up, swarms of small earthquakes), link each sign to the mechanism of rising magma, and grasp that eruption prediction combines several converging signs into a risk level or alert - it is evidence-based and probabilistic, not a guarantee of exact timing. The load-bearing insight is that good science here means reasoning under uncertainty: a false alarm, or a quiet volcano after a warning, can still reflect a sound decision rather than failure.
misconceptions: Scientists can predict the exact day/time of an eruption (they estimate risk/probability from evidence; timing is uncertain).
One warning sign means an eruption is certain (single signs are ambiguous; scientists combine several).
A false alarm means the scientists were wrong/bad at their job (acting under uncertainty means some false alarms and missed calls are unavoidable).
Monitoring stops eruptions (it can warn and reduce impacts, but cannot prevent the eruption).
If nothing has happened yet, the warnings were pointless (a non-eruption after warnings can be a correct low-probability outcome, not a mistake).

activities.title: In role with a volcanologist on duty
steps: Ask an in-role volcanologist the questions you really want answered: 'How do you know a volcano is about to erupt?', 'Can you tell me the exact day?', 'How sure are you?'

Have her show and explain the three main things she watches - gas emissions creeping up, the ground slowly bulging as magma pushes in, and swarms of tiny earthquakes - and why no single one is proof on its own.
Work through a Socratic challenge she poses, e.g. 'If only the gas rose but the ground stayed still, would you evacuate a town?' - give your reasoning out loud before she responds.
Discuss a real-type scenario: she once urged a town to evacuate and the volcano went quiet. Decide and argue whether that was a failure, then compare your view with her reasoning.
activities.insight: Prediction here means weighing several ambiguous signs together to judge a risk level - scientists act on the best evidence under uncertainty, so a false alarm can still be the right call.

activities.title: Make the call: an observatory monitoring panel
steps: Watch a set of gauges - gas level, ground tilt/deformation, and earthquake (seismicity) activity - change over a scenario.
Decide whether to raise or lower an alert level (e.g. green -> amber -> red) as the signals rise together or disagree.
Play through outcomes that include a false alarm and a missed sign, and read feedback framed as 'good decision under the evidence available', not simply right/wrong.
Explain afterwards which signals drove your call and how confident you could reasonably be.
activities.insight: Experiencing signals that rise together, conflict, or surprise you is intended to show that risk judgement draws on converging evidence and that uncertainty is built in, not a flaw.

activities.title: Explore and label a monitoring scene
steps: Examine a labelled observatory/volcano scene and tap or point to each instrument - gas sensor, tiltmeter, seismometer - to reveal what it detects and why it matters.
For each sign, state how it links to magma rising (magma pushing up -> more gas escapes, ground bulges, and small quakes occur).
Optionally note that scientists may also watch other signals, such as temperature changes, as extra evidence - without treating any single one as proof.
Answer a lift-the-flap style question - 'Can scientists be sure it will erupt?' - and check the response: 'No - they judge the risk from all the signs together.'
activities.insight: Builds the vocabulary and mechanism (what each instrument detects and why) as a foundation for the harder reasoning about combining evidence and uncertainty.

activities.title: Check understanding: signs, causes and what an alert means
steps: Match each warning sign to what it can indicate (rising gas emissions / ground swelling / earthquake swarms -> possibly magma moving up, though each can have other causes).

Answer selected-response questions such as 'In this activity's alert scale, what does a red alert issued before any eruption mean?', choosing 'the risk is judged high from the combined evidence' and rejecting the tempting distractor 'an eruption is certain'. (In some real alert systems, red can also be used once an eruption is already happening.)
activities.insight: A quick recognition check can confirm learners hold the key facts and the crucial distinction that a high alert issued before an eruption means high judged risk, not certainty.

checkQuestion: Volcanologists watch a volcano and say an eruption is 'likely soon' — but they can't say exactly when. How do they get evidence about what a volcano might do, and why can't they ever be completely certain about the day it will erupt?
checkAnswer: (Open — an epistemic probe, not a right/wrong answer.) A strong response surfaces: scientists gather several kinds of evidence (small earthquakes, ground swelling, gas emissions, temperature) and combine them, comparing with how this volcano and others behaved before past eruptions; but the inside of a volcano is hidden and every volcano behaves differently, so the signs make an eruption more or less LIKELY without fixing the exact time — prediction is about evidence and probability, not certainty.
